keyConcepts.title: Two ways to run the control plane
keyConcepts.text: **Per-router control** (each router runs the routing algorithm, as in OSPF and BGP) vs. **logically centralized control** (an SDN controller computes and installs the tables).

keyConcepts.title: Routing as a graph problem
keyConcepts.text: Routers are nodes and links are edges with costs c(x, y). The goal is the **least-cost path** between nodes.

keyConcepts.title: Link-state: Dijkstra
keyConcepts.text: Every node knows the whole topology (from link-state broadcast) and computes least-cost paths to all nodes in O(n²). With load-sensitive costs it can oscillate.

keyConcepts.title: Distance-vector: Bellman-Ford
keyConcepts.text: **d_x(y) = min_v { c(x,v) + d_v(y) }**. It's distributed, iterative and asynchronous. Good news travels fast, but bad news causes **count-to-infinity** (poisoned reverse only partly helps).

keyConcepts.title: Autonomous systems and OSPF
keyConcepts.text: The Internet is split into ASs for scale and administrative autonomy. **OSPF** is link-state routing inside an AS: admin-set link costs, authentication, equal-cost paths and areas with a backbone.

keyConcepts.title: BGP: the glue of the Internet
keyConcepts.text: Inter-AS routing to CIDR prefixes over TCP port 179 (eBGP between ASs, iBGP inside). Routes carry **AS-PATH** and **NEXT-HOP** attributes.

keyConcepts.title: BGP route selection and policy
keyConcepts.text: In order: highest **local preference** (policy), shortest **AS-PATH**, closest NEXT-HOP (**hot-potato**), then a tie-break. ISPs carry only traffic involving their customers.

keyConcepts.title: SDN control plane
keyConcepts.text: The controller has a southbound interface (OpenFlow), a network-state database and a northbound API for network-control apps. It reacts to events like link failures.

keyConcepts.title: ICMP
keyConcepts.text: Error reporting and diagnostics carried inside IP datagrams. Ping uses echo request/reply. Traceroute uses TTL-expired messages, then port unreachable at the destination.

keyConcepts.title: Network management
keyConcepts.text: **SNMP/MIB** queries and sets device data (with traps for events). **NETCONF/YANG** handles configuration with XML RPCs and atomic multi-device changes.

flashcards.back: Per-router: every router runs the routing algorithm. Centralized: an SDN controller computes and installs forwarding tables.
LS: every node has global knowledge of the whole topology. DV: each node knows only its neighbors' distance vectors.
**D(v) = min( D(v), D(w) + c(w,v) )** for each neighbor v of the newly added node w.
O(n²) in the worst case (n(n+1)/2 node checks).
With load-sensitive link costs, all routers shift traffic to the least-loaded path, which then becomes congested, and they switch back and forth.
**d_x(y) = min over neighbors v { c(x,v) + d_v(y) }**.

flashcards.front: When does a DV node send updates?
flashcards.back: When its own distance vector changes (because of a local link-cost change or a new vector from a neighbor).
After a link cost increases, DV estimates creep up slowly through routing loops, so it converges very slowly.
If z routes to x through y, z tells y its distance to x is infinity. It prevents two-node loops but not longer ones.
In LS, each node computes its own table, which limits damage. In DV, one bad node's wrong routes spread to the whole network.
Scale (too many routers for flat routing) and administrative autonomy (each ISP runs its own network).
Link-state routing inside an AS: flood link states, then run Dijkstra on the full map.

flashcards.front: How often does OSPF broadcast link state?
flashcards.back: Whenever a link changes, and at least every 30 minutes regardless.
An AS can be split into areas. Area border routers connect them through the backbone area.
eBGP: a BGP session between routers in different ASs. iBGP: a session between routers in the same AS.
Semi-permanent TCP connections on port 179.
The list of ASs an advertisement has passed through. It's used for path length and loop detection.
The IP address of the router interface that begins the AS-PATH (the neighboring AS's gateway).
Choose the gateway with the lowest intra-AS cost, to get packets out of your AS as cheaply as possible.
1) Highest local preference, 2) shortest AS-PATH, 3) closest NEXT-HOP (hot potato), 4) BGP identifier tie-break.
The same IP address is advertised via BGP from many locations, so users reach the nearest one. Used for DNS root servers.

flashcards.front: Why intra-AS and inter-AS routing differ
flashcards.back: Policy dominates between ASs; scale and performance are the focus within an AS.
Southbound: controller ↔ switches (e.g. OpenFlow). Northbound: controller ↔ network-control applications.

flashcards.front: OpenFlow messages from switch to controller
flashcards.back: Packet-in, Flow-Removed and Port-status.
Type 8 code 0 echo request; type 0 code 0 echo reply.
It sends packets with TTL 1, 2, 3…; each router where TTL expires returns ICMP type 11 (TTL expired).

flashcards.front: How traceroute knows it reached the destination
flashcards.back: The destination returns ICMP type 3 code 3 (port unreachable) because the probe used an unlikely UDP port.
An unsolicited message from an agent to the manager reporting an event (like a link going down).
NETCONF: the protocol (XML RPCs like get-config and edit-config over TLS). YANG: the data modeling language for that data.

quiz.q: Which routing approach needs every node to know the complete network topology?
quiz.explain: Link-state algorithms like Dijkstra use global knowledge obtained through link-state broadcast.

quiz.q: Node x has neighbors v (cost 2) and w (cost 5). v says its distance to y is 7; w says 3. What is d_x(y)?

options: Slow DV convergence after a link cost increases, caused by routing loops
quiz.explain: Bad news travels slowly in distance-vector, since neighbors keep pointing at each other while costs creep up.

options: Advertises an infinite distance to the neighbor you route through
Floods link states to all routers
quiz.explain: It prevents two-node routing loops, but loops involving three or more nodes can still form.

quiz.q: Which protocol is used for routing within an AS?
quiz.explain: OSPF (and IS-IS) are intra-AS link-state protocols. BGP is for routing between ASs.
BGP peers exchange routes over semi-permanent TCP connections on port 179. (IP protocol 89 is OSPF.)

options: Choosing the gateway with the lowest intra-AS cost
quiz.explain: Get packets out of your own AS as cheaply as possible, ignoring the cost beyond it.

quiz.q: What is BGP's FIRST route-selection rule?
quiz.explain: Policy comes first: local preference is set by the AS's administrators.

options: Several servers share one IP address advertised via BGP from different places
Packets are copied to all servers
quiz.explain: BGP routes each user to the 'closest' advertisement of the shared address.

quiz.q: In SDN, what does an OpenFlow port-status message tell the controller?
options: A port's state changed, such as a link going down
To install a new flow rule
A packet that matched no rule
quiz.explain: Port-status reports link changes. The controller's routing app then recomputes paths and updates flow tables.

quiz.q: Which ICMP message does a router send when a datagram's TTL expires?
quiz.explain: Traceroute relies on these type 11 messages to identify each router along the path.

options: An unsolicited message from an agent reporting an exceptional event
A request to set a MIB value
quiz.explain: Traps let devices notify the managing server without being polled.

quiz.q: What advantage does NETCONF have for configuration?
options: It can apply changes across multiple devices atomically
quiz.explain: Either all the changes succeed or none do, which avoids a half-configured network.
